title: introduce slab-grafting reclaimer and spill-rate cap to reduce KV cache fragmentation and spill storms
author: Jordan Keane
description: Motivation: In high-concurrency tenant workloads we continue to see transient spill storms driven by large numbers of small, fragmented slot allocations. These storms increase peak GPU memory usage and cause cascading evictions that harm latency. This PR introduces two orthogonal mitigations: (1) a slab-grafting reclaimer that coalesces adjacent free slots into larger usable extents with low CPU overhead, and (2) a spill-rate cap controller that rate-limits and smooths background spill operations to avoid sudden IO spikes. Design: slab-grafting is implemented as a background, incremental pass that scans per-shard free lists and attempts opportunistic graft operations when fragmentation score exceeds a threshold. Grafting is lock-free with respect to normal alloc/free paths by using a CAS-based two-phase promotion that marks ranges as 'staging' before atomically linking them into larger slabs. The spill-rate cap is a token-bucket controller in the KV spill scheduler; it enforces a soft cap on MB/sec of spill throughput and exposes a spill_smoothing_window_ms knob. When cap is hit, the scheduler prefers reclaiming contiguous grafted slabs and defers noncritical spill tasks. Compatibility: the grafting path is gated behind a runtime flag enable_slab_grafting and defaults off for older clusters; the spill cap has a conservative default of 128 MB/s but is tunable per-deployment and can be disabled. Testing: unit tests validate graft correctness across races and simulated concurrent frees; a stress harness (tools/kv_stress) demonstrates a 45% reduction in maximum concurrent spill IO during mixed-read/write tenant workloads, and a 12% P99 latency improvement on the generation path in our benchmark-lab scenarios. Rollout plan: staged canary to 10% of pods for 48h, monitor memory residency and spill_io_mbps metrics, then 50% for 24h, then global. Related work: follows the fragmentation detection work in ENG-3983 and complements the asynchronous compactor (ENG-4620). Known limitations: grafting is not effective for highly interleaved small live objects; in those cases we still rely on the compactor and eviction heuristics. Safety: feature flags and conservative defaults provided; metrics to watch: kv.fragmentation_score, kv.graft_ops, kv.spill_mbps, kv.eviction_count.

review_comments: Maya Patel (2026-02-16): Can you clarify the invariants around the 'staging' mark? I'm worried about a window where an allocator can see the range and try to reuse before graft completes.

Jordan Keane (2026-02-16): Answered: allocator checks a lightweight epoch bit and will fail allocation if range is marked staging; added comment and assertion to ensure allocation paths skip staging ranges.
Arjun Singh (2026-02-17): Performance nit: the graft scan poll interval defaults to 200ms; on our internal workloads that adds measurable CPU jitter. Can we make it adaptive (backoff when idle)?
Jordan Keane (2026-02-17): Implemented exponential backoff when graft rate drops below threshold; added tests and updated bench results.
release_notes:
- Added slab-grafting reclaimer to reduce KV cache fragmentation and improve allocation efficiency.
- Added configurable spill-rate cap to smooth spill IO and prevent spill storms.
- New metrics: kv.graft_ops, kv.graft_latency_ms, kv.spill_rate_limit_mb_s.
